currencies.headline: Sterling firm as traders price in higher odds of a BoE hike, not a cut.
currencies.commentary:
GBP has held up well over the past week as a rebound in oil prices, driven by renewed Middle East tensions, has pushed UK inflation expectations higher. Higher energy costs feed fairly directly into the UK's inflation basket, so when oil rallies, markets tend to reassess how much room the Bank of England actually has to cut rates further this year.

That reassessment has been fairly dramatic: a recent Reuters poll of economists found nearly 40% now expect at least one further Bank of England hike this year, a marked shift from earlier expectations of a rate cut. Markets are now pricing in the possibility of two hikes by March 2027. For context, sterling has generally taken its direction over the past year from the gap between UK and US/Eurozone interest rate expectations, so a more hawkish repricing of the Bank of England tends to support the pound relative to currencies where central banks are seen as more likely to ease.
currencies.watchToday: No major UK data due today, so sterling is likely to stay largely reactive to broader dollar and euro moves rather than its own news. Attention is building toward Thursday's Bank of England decision (Bank Rate currently 3.75%), where a new Monetary Policy Report will be published alongside the vote; that report's growth and inflation forecasts will matter as much as the rate decision itself for where sterling goes next.

currencies.headline: Euro steady after the ECB held rates last week.
currencies.commentary:
The ECB left its deposit rate unchanged at 2.25% at its 23 July meeting, keeping policy on hold amid ongoing energy-driven uncertainty. Christine Lagarde's post-meeting comments were read as fairly balanced, giving the market little fresh reason to move euro rate expectations in either direction.

With no ECB meeting scheduled this week, EUR direction is more likely to be driven by upcoming Eurozone growth and inflation data than by fresh central bank action. Germany's economy, as the bloc's largest, tends to have an outsized influence on how the euro reacts to Eurozone-wide releases, so growth or inflation surprises out of Germany specifically are usually worth watching a little more closely than the headline Eurozone figure alone.
currencies.watchToday: A quiet start to the week for the euro, with no major data releases scheduled today. ECB Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel, whose remarks are watched closely for any shift in tone on the path of rates, speaks tomorrow, followed by flash Q2 GDP and inflation data from Germany and the wider Eurozone later in the week, both of which have the potential to move EUR more than this week's speeches.

currencies.headline: Dollar in a holding pattern ahead of Wednesday's Fed decision.
currencies.commentary:
The Federal Reserve is widely expected to leave rates unchanged at 3.50%-3.75% this week, though markets are assigning a meaningful probability to a surprise hike given recent inflation pressure. That two-sided uncertainty is part of why the dollar has traded in a relatively tight range over the past few sessions. With a genuine chance of either outcome, investors have less conviction to push the currency firmly in one direction ahead of the announcement.

The press conference that follows Wednesday's decision will likely matter more than the rate decision itself for how USD trades afterwards, since that's typically where the Fed Chair gives the clearest signal on the likely pace and timing of any further moves this year.
currencies.watchToday: No major US releases today, leaving the dollar to take its cues mainly from positioning ahead of Wednesday. Consumer confidence data and a speech from Fed Governor Christopher Waller are due tomorrow, both of which could shift expectations one way or the other heading into the rate decision itself.

currencies.headline: Yen extends its slide to a fresh 40-year low ahead of Friday's BoJ decision.
currencies.commentary:
The yen has continued weakening against the dollar, touching a fresh four-decade low near 164 per dollar even as Japanese officials repeat warnings that they are ready to intervene if moves become disorderly. That warning has done little to slow the drop so far, a sign that broad dollar strength and a wide gap between US and Japanese interest rates are currently outweighing intervention risk in traders' minds.

Attention is turning to Friday's Bank of Japan meeting, where the BoJ is expected to hold rates steady but is under growing pressure to signal a faster path of future hikes. Inflation pressure has been building from the weaker yen itself, robust global demand tied to AI-related spending, and higher energy costs stemming from the Middle East conflict. A central bank holding rates but leaning hawkish in tone tends to matter more for direction than the decision itself, since it's the shift in expectations for future moves, not this week's outcome, that typically drives USD/JPY.
currencies.watchToday: Japan's national CPI print on Thursday will set the stage for Friday's Bank of Japan decision (rate currently 1.00%), where the central bank is expected to hold but may lean hawkish given the inflation pressure described above. Governor Ueda's post-meeting press conference will likely matter more for the yen than the decision itself.

currencies.headline: Franc holds firm near parity as the SNB keeps the door open to negative rates.
currencies.commentary:
The Swiss National Bank left its policy rate unchanged at 0% at its June meeting, as widely expected, while making clear that a return to negative rates has not been ruled out if the franc's strength and soft inflation persist. EUR/CHF has been trading durably below parity this year, reflecting the franc's traditional role as a safe haven at a time when Middle East tensions and elevated oil prices have kept broader risk sentiment fragile.

That safe haven demand is the key mechanism behind the franc's recent resilience: when geopolitical risk rises, investors tend to buy CHF regardless of what Swiss interest rates are doing, which is part of why the SNB has signalled greater readiness to intervene directly in the currency market rather than relying on rates alone. For clients, that means the franc can behave differently from other majors during periods of stress, often strengthening even as more growth-sensitive currencies come under pressure.
currencies.watchToday: No Swiss-specific data releases are being tracked this week; CHF trading is more likely to be driven by broader safe-haven flows tied to Middle East developments and this week's Fed decision than by anything scheduled domestically.

currencies.headline: Loonie steadies as rising oil offsets US tariff uncertainty.
currencies.commentary:
The Canadian dollar has firmed from last week's pullback, supported by a rally in oil prices as fighting around the Strait of Hormuz and threats from Yemen's Ansar Allah raise fresh concerns about Middle Eastern crude supply. The Bank of Canada held its overnight rate at 2.25% at its mid-July meeting while raising its 2026 inflation projection, and expects inflation to return to its 2% target by early 2027.

Oil remains one of the more reliable drivers of CAD given Canada's status as a major energy exporter, so the recent rally has provided some support even as fresh US tariffs on Canadian goods create a separate headwind. With those two forces pulling in opposite directions, USD/CAD has stayed range bound just above 1.40, and most bank forecasts see that easing only gradually over the coming months rather than moving sharply either way.
currencies.watchToday: No major Canadian releases are due today. With the Bank of Canada's next decision some weeks away, the loonie is likely to keep taking its cues mainly from oil prices and the broader dollar backdrop around Wednesday's Fed decision.

currencies.headline: Kiwi extends its rebound after the RBNZ's first hike in three years.
currencies.commentary:
The Reserve Bank of New Zealand raised the Official Cash Rate by 25 basis points to 2.50% on 8 July, its first hike since May 2023, and a stronger than expected inflation report released on 20 July has reinforced expectations of further tightening. Annual consumer price inflation accelerated to 4.1%, driven largely by a surge in fuel prices tied to the Middle East conflict, with petrol up more than 27% year on year.

Analysts now expect the RBNZ to hike again at both its September and October meetings, taking the OCR toward 3% by year end, which has helped the kiwi hold most of its recent gains. New Zealand's reliance on imported oil is a genuine vulnerability though: further escalation in the Middle East would push fuel costs, and inflation, higher still, but could also dent risk appetite in a way that weighs on a currency that tends to trade like a barometer for broader global sentiment.
currencies.watchToday: No New Zealand data is due today. With the next RBNZ meeting not until September, the kiwi is likely to stay reactive to broader dollar moves and Wednesday's Fed decision rather than its own news this week.

currencies.headline: Aussie tests the 0.70 handle as traders lift bets on an RBA hike.
currencies.commentary:
AUD/USD has been trading close to 0.7010, supported by growing expectations that the Reserve Bank of Australia will raise rates again, with markets now pricing roughly a one in four chance of a move at the RBA's August meeting and better than even odds by December. Firmer domestic activity data has added to that repricing over the past week.

China's economic performance remains the other major swing factor for the Australian dollar, since China buys around a third of Australia's exports and is the key source of demand for iron ore, coal and gas. China's economy grew 4.3% year on year in the second quarter, its weakest pace in three years, a reminder that a soft Chinese growth backdrop can offset even a hawkish RBA. For now, AUD/USD looks likely to stay within a broad 0.69 to 0.73 range.
currencies.watchToday: No major Australian data is due today, though this week's Fed decision and any fresh signal on China or commodity demand are likely to matter more for AUD than domestic news, ahead of Australian inflation and labour data due before the 11 August RBA meeting.

currencies.headline: Yuan holds steady as Beijing deepens Hong Kong's role as an offshore hub.
currencies.commentary:
The offshore yuan has been broadly stable this month after the People's Bank of China announced a set of structural measures aimed at cementing Hong Kong's position as the main offshore centre for yuan trading, including higher caps on cross border bond and currency facilities. Governor Pan Gongsheng said international demand for the yuan is broadening beyond simple trade settlement into investment and reserve holdings, though the PBoC gave no fresh signal on near term rate cuts.

The PBoC's approach continues to prioritise stability over sharp moves in either direction, managing the currency mainly through its daily fixing rather than large rate changes, which is why CNY tends to be one of the least volatile major currencies clients trade day to day. Several banks expect gradual yuan strength over the rest of 2026, but any shift usually plays out over weeks and months rather than in a single session.
currencies.watchToday: No CNY-specific events are being tracked this week; the yuan's daily fixing and any fresh PBoC commentary on Hong Kong's offshore role remain the main things to watch, alongside broader dollar direction around Wednesday's Fed decision.

currencies.headline: Rand nears R17 as a hawkish Fed and rising oil weigh on the currency.
currencies.commentary:
USD/ZAR has pushed through the R16.50 level and is approaching R17, a two month low for the rand, as a more hawkish Federal Reserve stance and rising oil prices linked to Middle East tensions both work against emerging market currencies like the rand. The South African Reserve Bank left its repo rate unchanged at 7.00% at its July meeting, a decision passed on a split 4 to 2 vote, despite markets having expected at least a quarter point hike.

South African inflation accelerated to 5.0% in June, which puts the SARB in a difficult position: raising rates further would support the currency but risks weighing on an already fragile growth outlook, while holding steady, as it just did, leaves the rand more exposed to swings in broader risk appetite and the dollar. As an oil importer, South Africa is also directly exposed to the recent rise in crude prices, which adds further inflation pressure at an awkward moment.
currencies.watchToday: No SARB meeting is scheduled this week, so the rand is likely to stay driven by external factors, particularly Wednesday's Fed decision and any further moves in oil prices tied to the Middle East, rather than domestic news.
